svg.title: Short-term and long-term memory, and the four crossings between them
svg.desc: Two stacked regions separated by a highlighted dashed horizontal boundary. The upper region is inside the context window and holds short-term memory: a fixed strip for the system prompt with tool definitions, and below it the transcript of this run, which is rebuilt on every pass and lost when the run ends. A note inside the upper region states that all three crossing arrows start or end at the transcript, because the transcript is the only part of the window that changes during a run. The lower region is outside the window and holds what persists between runs. It contains two different things: long-term memory, meaning a store of facts you wrote down deliberately, and separately the customer's own system of record — their documents and records, which were never yours and are not memory. Both persist between runs, which is the only property they share. A dashed arc above the upper region represents compaction, which summarises what is in the window and restarts the window with that summary, without ever leaving the window. Three arrows cross the boundary. A highlighted downward arrow is the write: the one fact that must outlive the run. An upward arrow is recall, reading that fact back at the start of a later run. A second upward arrow is retrieval, bringing in only the chunks the current question needs. A footer states that none of the four crossings happens by itself; each is a decision made in code, and each can drop the thing that mattered.

svg.text: Nothing crosses the orange line by itself. Compaction, the write, the recall and the retrieval are four decisions you make in code,

text.font-family: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace

svg.text: and every one of them can drop the thing that mattered. That is why this day is about deciding, not about storage.
